title: Turing computation and recursive functions

based_on.title: Computation Theory
based_on.venue: University of Cambridge, Part IB lecture slides, based on Andrew Pitts's notes
based_on.pages: Slides 82–83, 92–98 (composition, register hygiene, primitive recursion and sequential minimization, including the loop diagrams)

summary: Compile the finite-arity recursive closure rules into elementary counter programs and then into native tape machines, preserving undefined inputs.
abstract: Repeated addition needs a counter for the number of additions and a place to save the current answer. A program limited to adding one, testing and subtracting one, and halting can manage this information, provided copying restores its source and temporary registers are cleared before reuse. This makes it possible to translate the rules defining partial recursive functions—composition, recursion and sequential search—into finite counter programs, with one fixed program working for all inputs. The search program waits for each test to finish, so an undefined earlier test blocks later candidates exactly as required by sequential minimization. Combining this construction with the explicit counter-to-tape simulation produces a native Turing machine for every unary partial recursive function, writing each input number as that many marks. The reverse simulation then shows that native Turing machines and partial recursion define the same unary partial functions, including the inputs on which computation never halts. This proved comparison of mathematical models is distinct from the Church–Turing thesis about every effective procedure.
